rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds within 42 min and reveal the overall retention window and any hold-eluting peaks. This gives a good first map of where peaks sit in phi and whether later runs should narrow the gradient window, change slope, or adjust temperature.

All compounds eluted well inside the gradient, so narrow the phi window to bracket the observed elution region and make the gradient shallower where the peaks actually are. This should spread the moderately close cluster around rows 5–7 while still keeping all 10 peaks within the gradient and improving the time term.

Resolution is already perfect, so the next step is to cut analysis time aggressively while checking whether the critical cluster is slope-sensitive. A steeper version of the successful broad window should show how much minR erodes when peaks are compressed and may improve CRF if resolution remains acceptable.

The critical 5–7 cluster is clearly slope-sensitive: 20 min fully resolved it, while 10 min over-compressed it. An intermediate gradient should recover enough resolution on that cluster while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve or improve the current best CRF.

At 14 min only one pair remains slightly under-resolved, while 20 min gives full resolution but costs time, so 16 min is the logical interpolation. This should test whether a small decrease in slope is enough to push the 6/7 pair over the threshold while keeping the time penalty minimal.

The remaining question is whether the critical 6/7 pair can be improved by selectivity rather than more time, since it was strongly slope-sensitive but is already near the threshold at 14 min. A modest temperature decrease may slightly reorder or spread that close pair while keeping the run in the zero time-penalty region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by shifting the critical overlap from 6/7 to 5/6, so test the opposite direction. A modest increase to 45 C may improve selectivity for that central cluster while keeping the run comfortably in the no-time-penalty region.

Temperature changes worsened the central selectivity, so return to 40 C and refine only slope. Since 16 min fully resolves all peaks but incurs a small time penalty and 14 min is slightly under-resolved, 18 min tests whether resolution stays maximal while the CRF remains competitive or better than 16 min.

The optimum appears to lie between 10 and 16 min, with 14 min best so far, so check the other adjacent grid point. This will define whether the CRF peak is sharp around 14 min or whether a slightly steeper gradient can retain a similar score with better speed.

The broad window works best, but the last peak is still far from the end of the gradient, so slightly lowering phi1 should make the gradient a bit shallower around the critical middle cluster without risking late elution. This directly tests whether a small narrowing of the upper phi limit can improve the 6/7 separation while staying in the same favorable time regime.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, suggesting the upper end of the gradient was still wider than needed. Step phi1 down once more to see whether a slightly shallower gradient further improves the critical 6/7 pair without pushing the late peak too far out.

With phi1 = 0.90 improving over 0.95 and 0.85, the current best region is around that upper limit. Testing the steeper 12 min version will show whether the narrowed window preserves enough resolution to beat 14 min by shortening the run while staying near the apparent optimum in phi1.

The best point so far is 14 min at phi1 = 0.90, and 12 min is too steep, so test the neighboring shallower slope. This should show whether a small increase in tG can lift the 6/7 pair toward full resolution without introducing enough time penalty to lose against the current best.

Slope and upper-window optimization are nearly exhausted, so use some remaining budget to probe whether a larger temperature change can improve selectivity in the critical middle cluster. A low-temperature extreme is worth testing because modest ±5 C shifts were unfavorable, and a stronger shift could move the close pair differently rather than just scale retention.

The 25 C extreme strongly altered selectivity, so the opposite extreme is the most informative remaining temperature test. If 60 C shifts the problematic pair away from the 40 C behavior rather than worsening it like 45 C did, it could reveal a better selectivity regime; otherwise it will confirm that 40 C is near-optimal.

The best result uses phi1 = 0.90 at 14 min and 40 C, so the remaining lever is the lower boundary. Raising phi0 slightly will trim time spent below the first peak’s effective elution range and may subtly redistribute spacing in the central cluster without much risk, since the first peak is still clearly retained.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved the best method, so continue in the same direction to see whether the lower gradient boundary was still unnecessarily low. The first peak remains retained enough that phi0 = 0.15 is a reasonable next step, and it may further optimize spacing in the critical middle cluster while keeping zero time penalty.

The best region now appears centered near phi0 = 0.10 and phi1 between 0.85 and 0.90. Combining the improved lower bound with the slightly narrower upper bound tests whether both adjustments together can further shallow the useful part of the gradient and nudge the critical 6/7 pair upward without incurring a time penalty.

You have already reached the maximum CRF, so this run should map the local optimum in case multiple methods tie at 1.000. Testing the neighboring point with a slightly higher phi0 checks whether the optimum is broad or whether phi0 = 0.10 is uniquely best within the zero-penalty region.

Since both phi0 = 0.10 and 0.15 at phi1 = 0.85 achieve the maximum CRF, probe one step higher to define the edge of the optimum plateau. The first peak is approaching the unretained region, so this is a good boundary test for how far phi0 can be raised before resolution or retention starts to degrade.

With the optimum plateau now bracketed in phi0, test the next lower phi1 to locate the upper-bound edge of that plateau. This should reveal whether phi1 = 0.85 is the true optimum or whether the gradient can be narrowed a bit further before time penalty or late-peak retention becomes detrimental.

Phi1 = 0.80 was too low at phi0 = 0.10 because of time penalty, but the tied optimum at phi0 = 0.15 elutes everything earlier. This checks whether shifting both bounds upward together restores a perfect CRF with the narrower window or confirms that phi1 = 0.85 is the lower edge of the optimum plateau.

You already have multiple maximum-CRF methods, so use the remaining budget to see whether a different selectivity regime can also achieve 1.000 at a steeper, potentially more efficient setting near the optimum window. Combining the best phi window with the cooler temperature that shifted selectivity before may reveal an alternate local optimum for the central cluster.

The optimum window is established, and the remaining unresolved question is whether the 1.000 plateau extends to a steeper gradient at the better of the tied phi settings. This is the most direct nearby test of whether the current maximum can be matched with a shorter programmed gradient or whether 14 min is the true slope threshold.

For the final run, bracket the optimum plateau on the shallow side at the globally best phi window. Since 12 min is too steep and 14 min gives 1.000, this confirms whether 14 min is the true local optimum or whether the maximum extends to a slightly longer gradient as well.
